Desired Asset allocation: 80% stocks / 20% bonds (but open to discussion given pension holdings; see below)Desired International allocation: 15% of stocks (I've always just guessed at this)80/20 may be fine, but if you're wondering whether this is too steep, consider one or more of the three Control Your Risk exercises below. The common recommendation I see for int'l exposure is 20-40% of stocks or nothing at all as <20% is not enough for meaningful diversification from a US-only position, so it's just clutter (don't bother and go with 0%). That's obviously not a hard line where 19% is useless and 20% is acceptable, and 15% is better than 10%, but I'm going to suggest bumping this up to 20% (see the discussion on Value of Int'l Diversification below the AA self-determination section).Control Your Risk1) Read the Wiki article for Assessing Risk Tolerance, take the Vanguard Investor Questionnaire, then tailor the asset allocation (AA) that was recommended by the quiz based on your knowledge of your personal risk tolerance having read the Wiki article.2) Alternatively (or in addition to), ask "How much of a drop in portfolio value as a % of total value can I handle?" cut that % in half to get standard deviation, then lookup that std. dev. on the X-Axis of the chart below, and finally scan up to see what AA that corresponds to. As an example, if you can only stomach a -24% drop in portfolio value, that's a ±12% std. dev, which corresponds to an AA of 60/40. The return you get is an average and you'll get what you get with your unique sequence of returns (there's a lot of variance in outcomes due to the associated volatility of stocks so it probably will NOT be the average, but something more or less).a. For a long time-frame (>10 years) AAs below 20% stock are dominated (red dots) by another AA with similar risk but higher reward (blue dots).b. The dotted line represents a hypothetical linear risk-reward from 100% stocks down to 100% bonds; the historical risk-reward curve has an improvement for risk-adjusted return due to the lack of correlation between stocks & bonds.3) Vanguard's Target Date Retirement Glide-Path Design is a also a good starting point for choosing an AA. The choice of a specific TDF year should not solely be based on age, but could be earlier or later than your expected retirement age based on your personal risk-tolerance. You're not necessarily picking a specific TDF fund, you're just getting an idea of how to change your AA over time to apply to your specific fund choices.Value of Int'l Diversity from USIn my view (not a consensus), there's essentially two camps among Bogleheads: a) Those that are on board with the global market cap weighting, which is about 60% US stock and 40% ex-US stock; and b) those that have a home bias (US will usually outperform), which is about 80% US stock and 20% ex-US stock (some even omit Int'l altogether and <20% is just clutter, not enough to meaningfully diversify). I'm in camp a) based on the chart below from JP Morgan Asset Management, the white paper from Vanguard, and the more recent article from Vanguard.Vanguard White Paper: International Equity - Considerations and RecommendationsVanguard Web Article: Making the case for international stock & bond allocationsApplies to bonds too...Vanguard White Paper on International Bonds - Van uses int'l bonds in their Target Retirement and LifeStrategy funds, so could extend the 3-Fund portfolio to a 4-Fund or swap BND to BNDW if you wanted the world-cap weight of US and ex-US bondsI asked Taylor, author of the 3-Fund Portfolio, about why int'l bonds were omitted and while I expected something about currency risk or higher default risk, relative to the expected reward, instead the response in a private message on 31-Jan-2025 was "I feel simplicity is more important than more diversification."Portfolio Size: $615kCurrent retirement assetsYour Current layout is a bit cluttered at 20 holdings and that seems to be because you're mirroring the AA in most accounts. Some simplification can be had by viewing all accounts as a unified portfolio rather than treating most accounts as an individual portfolio that each has to be rebalanced independently (much more work, so simplify!). Holding bonds in a Roth (FXNAX in His Roth 403b) is sub-optimal (highlighted in purple); the preferred placement for bonds is in a Trad tax-deferred account, so that that the Roth can be 100% stocks and maximize the tax-free earnings attribute of Roth account types. Most of your accounts have a Total US Stock Index, but her Trad IRA has an S&P-500 Index which will constrain what you can hold in Taxable (highlighted in yellow) if you ever need to hold retirement funds there (perhaps after forced RMDs at age 75, but you don't need to spend the RMD so you'd prefer to reinvest it in stocks in Taxable). If there's an S&P-500 index from any provider (Fido, Van, Schwab, Blackrock, etc.) they're all essentially following the same index, so if any one of them is in a tax-advantaged account you can't hold any of them in Taxable. Conversely, you can't hold a "substantially identical" Total US Stock Index in both Taxable and a tax-advantaged account (or spouse's account) or you'd have the potential for Wash Sales, but the "total" stock funds from different providers tend to follow different indexes (so VTI, ITOT, FSKAX, and SWSTX are probably not "substantially identical" in IRS lingo). Typically I see "total" stock in Taxable and S&P-500 in Trad/Roth (because many 401k/403b plans don't offer a "total" stock fund) -OR- I see S&P-500 in Taxable and "total" stock in all the other accounts. There's no other issues than the Roth holding bonds, the S&P-500 in Her Trad IRA, and the sheer number of holdings added unnecessarily to complexity and more work for rebalancing. Your current AA is about 85/15 with 19% of stocks in int'l.The Proposed layout gets bonds out of Roth, swaps Her Trad IRA from S&P-500 to Van Total US Stock (clears the way for S&P-500 in Taxable at some future point with no wash sale concerns), and simplifies from 20 holdings down to X. His Trad 403B is the largest account and that's where we'll put a 3-Fund Portfolio, of US Stock, Int'l stock, and bonds. All the int'l stock for the entire portfolio as well as all the bonds are in this one account, simplifying all other accounts to hold just US stock. You had about 70/30 split among nominal bonds and TIPS, that I retained. This layout adheres to Tax-Efficient Fund Placement, avoids wash sales if you ever want to hold S&P-500 in Taxable in the future,, and is simpler to manage (all rebalancing for the entire portfolio happens in just the Trad 403b). This exactly meets an AA of 80/20 with 20% of stocks in int'l and cuts your holdings in half from 20 down to 10."Simplicity is the master key to financial success." -- John C. BogleA template spreadsheet (not your data) to help with asset allocation assessment and rebalance planning is linked below. Make a copy in your local GoogleSheets space to edit (or download to your local machine if you have Excel); I don't grant Editor access to sheets in my personal Google space. It should only take about 10-30 minutes once a year to patch your balances and plan a shuffle among funds if any deltas are off by more than ±5% (or whatever your personal rebalance threshold is).Asset Allocation SheetAA Current and Proposed1a. My wife and I each have pensions. Mine is CALSTRS defined benefit as well as a supplemental which turns into an annuity upon retirement, paid out in 3, 5,or 10 years. My defined benefit will be about 65% or so of my retirement income. My wife will have less years into her CALPers plan. How do we factor in the pensions into our investments / portfolio holdings? I had read that they can be considered bond holdings, but I just don't get that.Her pension is for the rest of her life, but yours seems to only have 10 years as the longest option. My quick Google searching of CALSTRS notes that is pays a lifetime benefit, so could you clarify the statement "paid out in 3, 5, or 10 years?" Is that just a start-time after retiring or is that the pay out (only 3 years of payments or 10 years of payments)?For a defined benefit over N years, you can calculate the Present Value of the annuity payments and use that $ amount as a bond in your portfolio (see the Journal of Accountancy legacy article on Valuing an Annuity). I don't like that approach and don't recommend it because you can't sell this bond (to spend it) nor can you use it to rebalance your portfolio (can't buy as well as can't sell). It's a separate income stream that you don't control, and it certainly counts towards your total retirement income, but it's not a phantom bond in one's portfolio in my opinion. So I use it as an offset to the portfolio draw (which in the case of CALSTRS is maybe not a permanent offset?).I could run my Withdrawal Monte Carlo (MC) model, but I'm hesitant to do so without the following:a) a more verified estimate of retirement expenses;b) a $ value for the two pensions, as well as her SocSec and when you're both claiming that, and whether or not they're inflation-adjusted each year in retirement; andc) Desired life-expectancy for planning purposes (typically 95 but if either has a family history of shorter/longer lifespans you might want to use something other than age 95).All that info will improve the accuracy of the MC inputs, but MCs always produce a large range of outcomes, so then there's the risk-acceptance level you want to choose for planning (you'll probably get something near the median/50th percentile, but it's likely better to plan on a bad sequence of returns and use 10th or 20th and rejoice when you actually get something better, rather than plan on 50th and have a 50% chance of having to cut retirement spending to remain solvent for the remainder of the period).I will say your AA is likely fine unless you lose sleep at night over a possible market crash of -50% (in which case you probably want to adjust your AA to a lower stock %). Working longer before retiring and/or figuring out how to save more are going to be more impactful than tweaking your AA (so pick your AA for a good Sleep Well At Night or SWAN factor).Impact of 3 Investment Factors for Accumulation & WithdrawalOn getting a verification check against your budgeted expenses in retirement, start with @KlangFool's formula to estimate your current expenses: Annual Expenses = Gross Income (1040, Line 9) - Taxes (1040, Line 24 + State + Local + SocSec + Medicare) - Annual Savings (Roth 401k, Roth IRA & Taxable). Note that suggested accounting for annual savings does not include deductible Trad 401k/IRAs because those are already accounted for in 1040, Line 1 (from W-2, Box 1) which feeds Line 9. Then adjust that by what will change in retirement (retirement savings and SocSec/Medicare taxes go away, but savings for home repair/upgrade, fresh cars, gifts to children remain; principal & interest eventually go away when mortgage is paid off, but property tax & hazard insurance remain; commuting costs might go down but vacation spending might go up; term life insurance payments might go away but costs for long-term care in late retirement might go up).The beauty of Klang's formula is that if you take out taxes and known savings you are spending all the rest of it. We've seen posters that had a detailed budget in a spreadsheet or phone app and were surprised to see Klang's formula show them as much as $50K of unaccounted spending!You can tailor where taxes get accounted for (e.g., you could just consider it all as "retirement savings" or "lumpy expenses"), just make sure all your expenses are accounted for somewhere among taxes, savings, and monthly expenses. Don't forget stuff that gets deducted from your paycheck besides income taxes like health insurance, life insurance, pension contributions, etc.Again, I'm happy to help run a MC sim or a TPAW run, but you need to prove more details on retirement age for each, and expected "other income" streams ($/yr and when that age they kick in).1b. Follow up to #1a...as we move toward retirement, there are so many machinations to the pensions...do we get somebody to consult with that knows it backward and forward....an estate planner? Other help?There might be someone from CALSTRS (and CALPERS) that's available to consult with plan beneficiaries through your respective HR departments. If not Google for private consultants. Like @CyclingDuo mentioned, they got lucky as their Fido advisor was interested in this, but not all estate planners or financial planners are going to have deep knowledge of those two CA-specific plans. An advisor/consultant based in CA is more likely to be "in-the-know" concerning those pensions. I'd start with your own HR departments first, and then consider paying for an outside consultant if the folks HR connects you with do not answer all your questions.These are the materials from the pension plan providers.CALSTRS: Understand your benefitsCALPERS 101: Understanding your retirement system2. I figure my 403b's holding of international bond is a misclick. Change that to US bond, right?As @CyclingDuo noted, int'l bonds are part of int'l diversification (it's both stocks & bonds) used in Van TDFs and LifeStrategy funds. Taylor just omitted them from the 3-Fund Portfolio for simplicity and that's fine, but if you want regional diversification for bonds, you can shift from a 3-Fund to a 4-Fund portfolio (in your case 5-Fund because you've decided to hold TIPS).3. Anything else we should be doing differently as I move toward retirement? I figure we should be saving more but, damn, CA w/ kids is expensive. I think I have to do 4 more years in the pension to get to some 30 year calculation bonuses, which is a bummer, but is what it is.Saving more does help, but working a few more years at your current savings rate is more impactful (see the impact of 3 factors chart earlier under questions #1a). Since the accumulation part seems a little more straight-forward than the withdrawal part (complicated by the pensions and her SocSec), we can take a quick look at that.For an initial balance of $615K, an AA of 80/20 (fixed), a contribution period of "4 more years," and a contribution amount of $27.8K/yr (increasing by +3%/yr for raises/inflation), then the range of balance-at-retirement looks something like this by percentile:End-BalPercentile$707.6K 10th$806.3K 20th$1,028.6K 50th$1,261.9K 80th$1,394.5K 90thYou'll probably get something around $1M (50th percentile), but for planning it's likely better to assume a bad sequence of returns (SOR) by choosing 10th percentile. If your risk tolerance is high maybe you could plan on 15th or 20th percentile. The 10th percentile balance of about $710K supports a 3.7% initial draw (down from the "4% for 30 years" rule, because your withdrawal period is a bit longer at 35 years from ages 60-95) of about $26.2K, which is $23.3K in today's $. So if CALPERS + CALSTRS + Portfolio ($23.3K) + SocSec ($??? later) > Taxes + Post-Retirement Savings + Monthly Expenses + Discretionary, then you're golden. Otherwise, you'll need to work longer, save more, and/or figure out how to cut expenses. This is a rough cut and it's likely more informative to do the withdrawal MC with specific offsets to the portfolio draw for the two pensions, and then later SocSec for your two claiming ages. On optimal claiming ages, take a look at https://opensocialsecurity.com, which often recommends the lower earner claim at 62 while the higher earner claims at 70.That 3.7% initial draw with adjustment for inflation thereafter is a Const-$ withdrawal strategy per the Trinity Study. While it can feel good to have a 90% likelihood of being able to draw an ever-increasing amount from the portfolio for at least 35 years, there are alternative withdrawal methods that allow you to spend more during your lifetime (leaving a smaller residual to heirs/charity) such as Variable Percentage Withdrawal (VPW) or the TPAW Planner's Amortization Based Withdrawal (ABW is is recalculated each year by TPAW, so also a variable strategy). If discretionary is say at least 1/3 of total expenses, then VPW or ABW might be a better strategy for you.Here's my Accumulation Monte Carlo results for the predicted balance range 4 years from now.Data and Models I use for Monte Carlo:NYU Data Set 1928-2017 with Model FitsAccumulation Monte Carlo <- Image aboveWithdrawal Monte CarloYou'll need a MS Excel license; download to your local machine and enable macros (required for the 1,000 random trials and results aggregation).I'm using my own model as I like to know what's under the hood, but there are other models I like that have public facing website interfaces:TPAW Planner (probably most comprehensive, supports ABW), <- Try this one!Portfolio Visualizer's Monte Carlo (also their Financial Goals model is nice),Engaging Data: Rich, Broke, or Dead, (uses historical returns in a cycle for your retirement duration), andFireCalc (also historical data, but lots more inputs to tailor to your situation).Paid models sometimes cited here include Boldin, Pralana Gold, and ProjectionLab as well as many others (just citing these not recommending for or against on any of these).That 10th percentile result represents a bad SOR (e.g., multiple years with bad returns, perhaps as low as a -60% crash). The uncertainty in projected balance tends to grow exponentially with the duration of the accumulation/withdrawal period (the longer you're saving or withdrawing the bigger the variance between the 10th and 90th percentiles). However, if some/most of your spending in retirement is discretionary then VPW or ABW withdrawal strategies largely mitigate the SOR risk (in exchange for a cut in spending which reduces inflation-adjusted purchasing power, but you'll never run out of money early with VPW and it's much less likely to run out with ABW vs about 10% risk of running out early with Const-$).Standard caveats about simulations apply. Those using 30y rolling periods suffer from small sample size for estimating a binomial proportion as the success rate and can potentially indicate counter-intuitive results (e.g., implying higher stock exposure will reduce risk of running out early; FICalc was showing this and it's probably just an anomaly of the specific 30y rolling periods, skewed by the latest 15 years having phenomenal stock returns). Those using a large sample size as random draws from a distribution assume the distribution is constant over the withdrawal period. All sims suffer from assuming the future looks like the past in one way or another."All models are wrong, some are useful." – George E. P. Sources indicate that ARVA is amortization by another name.You amortize the portfolio on top of the floor over the remaining N years with a fixed discount rate, and you re-amortize every year. You'd get the exact same results in ABW. This is not a diss on thebestthird and Shardansky's paper. That method is a special case of TPAW (off portfolio income, specific constant future stocks average return, fixed AA at 100% stocks) and I'm a huge fan and user of TPAW. What I find interesting (and still looking at) is how the floor is handled when it has a horizon of over 30 years, since there are no TIPS past that point.I don't see best third as a special case of TPAW. I see ARVA, the bestthird approach, TPAW, ABW and countless others as merely particular implementations of an amortization approach to withdrawals from a portfolio. The differences usually have to do with the choices of discount rates/expected returns, whether or not there is an attempt to keep total portfolio risk constant throughout retirement, whether or not future cash flows (like a pension or social security) are considered by discounting them back to the present as well as other features such as spending tilts, income floors, etc. Seemingly endless possibilities and choices that different folks might be interested in and depending on whether they want to roll their own spreadsheet or whether they're OK with whatever is available off-the-shelf, whether free or not. The oldest mention I've found so far of using amortization for this was in a paper back in 2012 from "Bud" Hebeler, "Withdrawal Strategies in Difficult Times", available here: (see page 2, method 2 in the middle of the page) http://www.analyzenow.com/Articles/Strategy ... -22-12.pdfHe has no footnotes, but it wouldn't surprise me if the idea had been around even longer, maybe even before spreadsheets were available.There are ways to handle a floor over 30 years. First, by definition, the SS portion of the floor is essentially a lifetime annuity. But Kevin M has shown a way with his toolset to extend a TIPS past 30 years since some of the longer TIPS which have durations past 30 years. It would require some maintenance (buying/selling TIPS) for a while until you got to the point where all you needed was the 30 year set and forget ladder. Alternatively, the non ladder portion of the portfolio could be used to extend the ladder one year at a time by selling risky assets and buying another rung. There is interest rate risk in doing that of course.Cheers.Statistics: Posted by dcabler — Thu Nov 26, 2026 3:24 pm.

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

“It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

In a recent development, “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

In a recent development, vasiliev mentioned that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

According to recent reports, baia states the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no latest soft snow had accumulated.

In a recent development, the Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#136798. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1288 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing fresh route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing fresh route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin mentioned. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Industry observers note that bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

Recent findings suggest that this was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” stated Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he noted.

It has been revealed that there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

According to recent reports, if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Sources indicate that red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Industry observers note that once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

It has been revealed that thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” mentioned Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

Recent findings suggest that that said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they noted. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the substantial cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

Industry observers note that to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

It has been revealed that marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

Sources indicate that “That is why it is key to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

Industry observers note that the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they noted. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he noted.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they noted.

Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

Recent findings suggest that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

Sources indicate that the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” remarked Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

According to recent reports, by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • It has been revealed that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

It has been revealed that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

It has been revealed that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

It has been revealed that interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Industry observers note that ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed strategy.

According to recent reports, despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Industry observers note that keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

It has been revealed that at the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#136788. Senate Passes BAAJA, the Massive Permitting Bill That Will Expedite Development on Public Lands

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (663 w)

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Senate Passes BAAJA, the Massive Permitting Bill That Will Expedite Development on Public Lands

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A controversial bill aimed at speeding up infrastructure projects on public lands passed the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that the Senate declined to vote on a flurry of last-minute amendments to the nearly 500-page text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — including one that would have banned data centers on public land, before voting for the third time late Thursday night.
  • Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A controversial bill aimed at speeding up infrastructure projects on public lands passed the U.S. Senate Thursday night and now heads to the House.

Sources indicate that the Senate declined to vote on a flurry of last-minute amendments to the nearly 500-page text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — including one that would have banned data centers on public land, before voting for the third time late Thursday night. Support in the Senate eroded over the series of votes, from 73-25 on the first vote Nov. 9 to a final vote of 62-33. A bill requires a simple majority of 51 votes in the Senate to pass.

Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

BAAJA is co-sponsored by Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from New Mexico often considered a conservation champion, and Sen. Mike Lee, the Utah Republican and architect of recent attempts to sell public land. Heinrich says BAAJA cuts red tape and will speed up renewable energy projects to help fight climate change, increase jobs, and bring down energy costs for average Americans.

Conservation advocates, however, fear it will also lock in projects many sportsmen and women have spent years fighting, like a copper-sulfide mine by the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or the Pebble Mine in Alaska’s Bristol Bay. It also may well open the door for massive data centers on public land, something most of the conservation and sporting community resoundingly oppose.

“I understand this is a big, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life earlier this week.

BAAJA proponents say it increases project certainty. Right now, one administration can reverse or cancel permits approved by a prior administration. But by limiting the back and forth between administrations the bill also drastically changes how much oversight a project can receive, even under foundational laws like the Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act and National Historic Preservation Act. The bill will also limit public input into projects and judicial overview.

Many of the nation’s tribes have forcefully spoken out against the bill saying it severely curtails tribal input.

Recent findings suggest that “Overall, the bill, by weakening these bedrock laws, would make it far easier to fast-track AI data centers as well as fossil fuel, mining, and other extractive infrastructure. Once these projects are approved, they would be difficult to unwind,” according to the Western Environmental Law Center. “BAAJA would cause grave, generational harm to the West’s public lands, waters and wildlife, and communities.”.

Heinrich has stated he opposes data centers on public land.

“To be clear, BAAJA is federal legislation focused on energy infrastructure and grid connectivity,” a spokesperson told OL in an emailed satement. “It does not ‘permit’ data centers on public lands. State and local government approval is still required. The Senator’s legislation addresses the federal energy infrastructure challenges associated with a grid that cannot keep up with demand; it does not circumvent the state and local processes that determine whether specific projects move forward.”.

Even conservation groups who support portions of the bill question how fast such a massive piece of legislation is moving through Congress. This is the first major permitting reform bill in decades and was introduced Sept. 30.

Read Next: Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Proposal Really Means for Outdoorsmen.

The bill now heads to the House. If representatives make any changes to the Senate version, the Senate must vote again on the bill before it heads to President Trump’s desk for his signature. The president has said he supports the bill.

In a recent development, this story was updated on Nov. 20 at 2:30 p.m. CST to include comment from Sen. Heinrich’s office.

School Teacher’s First Deer with a Bow Is This 226-Inch Illinois Giant

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that southern Illinois school teacher Darin Hicks grew up in a hunting family, but he didn’t start hunting deer himself until just a few years ago.
  • “I started seeing a large buck, but never in the day [at first],” the 40-year-old Illinois native tells Outdoor Life.
  • Hicks was mentoring his 9-year-old daughter, Josie, who wanted her first deer to be a buck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that southern Illinois school teacher Darin Hicks grew up in a hunting family, but he didn’t start hunting deer himself until just a few years ago. As his interest in deer hunting grew, he took special notice of any major bucks he spotted during his daily drives to and from school as a science teacher.

“I started seeing a large buck, but never in the day [at first],” the 40-year-old Illinois native tells Outdoor Life. “We don’t use trail cameras. But I got plenty of [phone] photos the last couple years of a really good buck — but only a few photos during the day.”.

Hicks was mentoring his 9-year-old daughter, Josie, who wanted her first deer to be a buck.

Sources indicate that “I had her out in youth season, and she could have taken a lot of does but wanted a buck. One evening we saw a buck, but it was too dark [even though it was still legal light] and Josie didn’t want to shoot in that poor light.”.

Hicks thinks the buck that he and his daughter spotted that evening during the youth season may have been the giant buck he arrowed weeks later.

In a recent development, on Nov. 14 he hung a ladder stand near a wooded thicket full of rubs, scrapes, and plenty of trails. He set the stand for his dad, 77, to hunt during the upcoming Illinois gun opener on Nov. 20.

But that Saturday night Hicks’ wife, Katie, asked her husband if he wanted to bowhunt the stand the next day, before his father got in it the following week.

According to recent reports, hicks noted there wasn’t much time that next morning on Sunday before they left for church. Katie said he had a good two hours to hunt from dawn until leaving for church with his family.

She had a good point, Hicks decided, and climbed into the stand the following morning of Nov. 15.

He sat for about an hour and spotted a doe with twin fawns at 150 yards. Suddenly the doe with young spooked and out stepped the giant buck Hicks had seen from afar for the last two years.

“I was shaking, found my grunt call and blew it once,” he says. “He turned and started walking toward me and my heart was pounding overtime.”.

The buck came steadily closer while Hicks readied for a shot — the first time he would ever draw his bow on a whitetail.

It has been revealed that “He walked toward me, stopped, and looked up at me at 15 yards, then he turned to head away,” Hicks says. “He started through some brush quartering away at 35 yards and I drew, released, and I heard a loud smack.”.

The buck collapsed in his tracks. Hicks’ arrow had hit a bit high, but his 2-blade mechanical struck the spine and the buck didn’t get up.

Recent findings suggest that hicks managed to wrestle the nontypical out of the woods and, field-dressed, it weighed 187 pounds. His taxidermist aged the buck at 5 1/2 years, with a gross green score of 226 1/8 inches.

Read Next: Complete Shock.’ Long-Haul Trucker Hunter Tags 227-Inch Nontypical During State Park Hunt.

“We all still made it to church that morning,” Hicks says. “And I even got to teach Sunday School.”.

#136783. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1694 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • Industry observers note that the journey has not gone according to strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

Industry observers note that the journey has not gone according to strategy. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid intends. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

Industry observers note that by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and strategy ahead.

It has been revealed that the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line demonstrates the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

Recent findings suggest that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with latest designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

It has been revealed that food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

According to recent reports, safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

Sources indicate that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

According to recent reports, we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Recent findings suggest that successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

In a recent development, the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

In a recent development, you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

According to recent reports, I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Sources indicate that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

Industry observers note that the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

Industry observers note that the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

You can follow the expedition here.

💪 Into the High Sierra: ❄️ Snow, Ice & Forrester Pass 🏔️

💡 Key Takeaways
